title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
description: A direct, already-optimal stack-based evaluation of postfix notation, with careful attention to operand order and truncating division.

blocks.text: Given an array of strings tokens representing an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation (postfix notation), evaluate it. Valid operators are +, -, *, and /. Each operand may be an integer or another expression. Division between two integers should truncate toward zero. It is guaranteed the expression is always valid.

blocks.caption: Numbers push onto a stack; an operator pops the two most recent operands, computes, and pushes the result back

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Reverse Polish (postfix) notation, where operators come AFTER their operands","A stack naturally evaluates postfix notation: numbers push, operators pop their operands, compute, and push the result"],["Order matters for non-commutative operators (subtraction, division)","The FIRST popped value is the RIGHT-hand operand, the SECOND popped is the LEFT-hand operand, since a stack reverses insertion order"]]}

blocks.text: In postfix notation, an expression like "2 1 +" means "add 2 and 1" (the operator comes after its two operands); more complex expressions nest naturally, since each operator always applies to whatever two values were MOST RECENTLY computed or given, exactly matching a stack's behavior.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Calculator That Only Ever Operates on the Last Two Numbers Entered
blocks.text: Imagine a calculator where entering a number simply remembers it, and pressing an operator button (+, -, *, /) immediately combines the two MOST RECENTLY entered (or computed) numbers, replacing them with the result. This is exactly how postfix notation is evaluated: a stack naturally tracks "the most recently available values," which is exactly what each operator needs to combine.

blocks.caption: A number token is pushed directly; an operator token pops the two most recent values (b then a) and pushes a OP b back

blocks.text: Since postfix notation is DEFINED by "an operator applies to whatever two values came most recently before it," a stack directly and naturally evaluates the expression in a single linear pass.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Postfix notation never needs parentheses or operator precedence rules, since the ORDER of tokens already fully determines exactly which values each operator combines: always the two most recently available ones.

Observation 2: A number token is simply pushed, becoming available for a future operator.

Observation 3: An operator token pops exactly two values, computes the result, and pushes it back, making that combined result available for any LATER operator to use, exactly modeling how sub-expressions nest in postfix notation.

Observation 4: For non-commutative operators (subtraction and division), the pop ORDER matters: the value popped FIRST is the operator's RIGHT-hand operand (it was pushed later, so it is more recent), and the value popped SECOND is the LEFT-hand operand.

Observation 5: After processing every token, the stack contains EXACTLY one value: the final answer.
This is a direct stack-based evaluation: numbers push, operators pop their two most recent operands (in the correct order), compute, and push the result back.
Process the tokens left to right using a stack: push numbers directly, and for each operator, pop the two most recent values (in the correct order) and push the computed result.

items: Walk through the tokens: if a token is a number, push it onto the stack.
If a token is an operator, pop the top TWO values (b, then a), compute a OP b, and push the result back onto the stack.
After all tokens are processed, the single remaining value on the stack is the answer.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Popping b BEFORE a is crucial: since b was pushed (or computed) more recently, it represents the operator's RIGHT-hand side, essential for correctly evaluating subtraction and division.
This IS already the standard optimal approach for this problem; there is no meaningfully "slower" alternative worth comparing against, since a stack directly matches postfix notation's structure.

blocks.text: Correctly evaluates any valid postfix expression, since the stack-based approach directly mirrors postfix notation's defining structure.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass through the tokens.
Space: O(n), for the stack in the worst case (a long sequence of numbers before any operators).
This approach is already optimal for this problem; there is no meaningful further optimization beyond correctly implementing the direct stack-based evaluation.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Since the direct stack-based approach is already the natural and optimal solution for postfix evaluation, "optimizing" here means ensuring the implementation correctly handles every subtlety: the pop order for non-commutative operators, and truncating (not flooring) integer division toward zero.

Walk through tokens with a stack. For a number, push it (after parsing). For an operator, pop b then a, compute a OP b (using truncating division, not floor division, for "/"), and push the result. Return the single remaining stack value at the end.
Process each token directly against a stack, carefully preserving operand order and using truncating (not flooring) division.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The final stack contains just 22, matching the expected result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single linear pass.
Space: O(n), for the stack in the worst case.

Postfix notation is constructed so that at every operator token, exactly the two most recently available values (numbers or previously-computed sub-results) are its intended operands; a stack naturally provides exactly "the two most recently available values" via two pops, making the evaluation direct and unambiguous, with no need for parentheses or precedence rules.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A number token","Pushed directly onto the stack"],["A commutative operator (+, *)","Order of the two popped operands does not affect the result"],["A non-commutative operator (-, /)","The FIRST popped value (b) is the right-hand side, the SECOND (a) is the left-hand side: computed as a OP b, not b OP a"]]}

items: Checking whether a token is one of the four operator symbols (versus attempting to parse it as a number) correctly distinguishes operators from operands.

Truncating division toward zero (rather than using a language's default floor division, which rounds toward negative infinity for negative results) is essential, since some languages' default behavior differs from the problem's specified truncation rule.
The single remaining stack value at the end is guaranteed to be the final answer, since the problem guarantees the expression is always valid.

blocks.text: Postfix (Reverse Polish) notation is DESIGNED to be evaluated with a stack: an operator always combines the two most recently available values, with no need for parentheses or precedence rules, making the stack-based evaluation both natural and optimal.

items: Popping the two operands in the WRONG order for subtraction or division, silently producing an incorrect result for non-commutative operations.
Using a language's default integer division (which may round toward negative infinity) instead of explicitly truncating toward zero as the problem specifies.
Forgetting to handle multi-digit or negative number tokens correctly when parsing (e.g., "-11" is a single negative number token, not a subtraction operator followed by 11).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["A single number with no operators at all","The result is simply that number"],["Division resulting in a negative fractional value (e.g., -7 / 2)","Truncates toward zero, giving -3 (not -4, which is what floor division would give)"],["Deeply nested sub-expressions","The stack naturally handles any nesting depth, since each computed sub-result simply becomes available for a later operator"]]}

items: Explicitly calling out the "truncate toward zero, not floor" division rule and the correct pop order for non-commutative operators up front avoids two of the most common silent-bug pitfalls in this problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Evaluate an expression in Reverse Polish / postfix notation" points directly and unambiguously to a stack-based evaluation.

items: How would you convert an INFIX expression (with parentheses and precedence) to postfix notation first? The Shunting Yard algorithm, itself also stack-based, handles this conversion, after which this same evaluation technique applies directly.

How would you handle floating-point numbers instead of integers? The same stack-based approach applies directly; only the division truncation rule would no longer be needed (floating-point division would just work normally).

How would you extend this to support additional operators (e.g., exponentiation, modulo)? Simply add another case to the operator-handling logic, following the exact same pop-two-compute-push pattern.

The foundational stack-based expression evaluation pattern, related conceptually to Basic Calculator II elsewhere in this category, which evaluates a more complex INFIX expression using similar stack-based principles.
